title: AI assists audit pre-planning, risk brainstorming, walkthrough notes and starting risk scores
problem: Pre-planning research, risk brainstorming, scoping and walkthrough notes take time before testing starts, and the annual risk assessment starts from a blank page.
approach: A Gartner poll finds 60% of audit professionals use generative AI for engagement pre-planning and 44% for planning (independent).
Grant Thornton published 16 sample agent instructions for internal audit; Optro announced agentic risk-assessment scoring that recommends starting scores with supporting evidence.
SOX leaders on a May 2026 panel described assistive uses and reported few autonomous ones.
The auditor validates AI-surfaced risks and confirms or overrides each starting risk score before the plan is issued.
who: Gartner poll, Grant Thornton, Optro, KPMG

title: Board materials and risk registers turned into audit actions between planning cycles
problem: Board packs, audit actions and remediation tracking live in separate places, so signals in governance materials do not become audit follow-up.
approach: Diligent links AuditAI to Smart Prep 360, which reviews board materials for anomalies and control gaps; AuditAI turns signals into evidence requests.
Using AI to sense risk themes between planning cycles is discussed as an idea. No outcome figure is published.
The chief audit executive and risk leaders decide what enters the risk register and audit plan.

title: AI drafts risk-control matrices, test procedures and request lists for review
problem: Building a risk and control matrix from notes and diagrams takes an auditor days, and writing test steps, sampling and evidence lists is repetitive.
approach: RSM describes an agent that reads process documents, drafts the risk and control matrix, writes test procedures and produces a request list.
An RSM director says a first-draft matrix takes minutes versus one to two days (self-reported); in acceptance testing it sometimes merged controls.
Grant Thornton's CompliAI, deployed February 2024, drafts control narratives and test steps; it says tasks take minutes, not days (self-reported).
The auditor reviews and corrects the matrix and procedures before testing and before they go to control owners.

title: Agents prepare evidence requests, check submissions and chase follow-ups
problem: Loosely worded information requests and long waits for data slow fieldwork, and incomplete evidence is found weeks later as follow-up trails go cold.
approach: In a co-sourced billing audit, Baker Tilly used Fieldguide agents to prepare requests, link them to audit objectives and track status.
Baker Tilly says AI reduced coordination time and improved coverage (self-reported); Diligent reports about 70% less administration time among early adopters (vendor-published).
Crown Castle's audit manager says AuditAI cut evidence-chasing time by more than half (vendor-published).
The auditor remains responsible for procedure, evidence, analysis and conclusion.
who: Baker Tilly, Fieldguide, Diligent, Crown Castle

title: In-house audit teams hand SOX testing to agents, with review (Reddit, Klaviyo)
problem: SOX testing is repetitive and getting heavier: KPMG's survey reports testing hours per control rose from 12 to 16 and SOX maintenance cost rose 45%.
approach: Optro's Autonomous Testing agent reads evidence, tests each attribute and writes the result with a citation trail; the auditor signs off.
Optro says Reddit automated 175 controls in three months and cut testing time per control by 60% on average (vendor-published).
Reddit has since expanded agentic testing to over 75% of its SOX controls (vendor-published).
The auditor reviews and approves each test conclusion and every exception.

title: Advisory firms run agentic control testing inside co-sourced and outsourced audit engagements
problem: Co-sourced SOX testing is sold on hours, evidence arrives in mixed formats, workpapers must stand up to the external auditor, and clients want shorter cycles.
approach: RSM Beacon, with Andera, allocates evidence to samples, tests attributes and writes an annotated workpaper; ambiguous items go to a human.
Riveron, Protiviti (Fieldguide alliance) and PwC (Dynamic Testing) also run agents at defined methodology steps.
PwC says effort can fall 30-40% and turnarounds shrink from weeks to days (vendor-published; no sample given).
Experienced professionals review every test result before it enters the workpaper.

title: Risk-advisory teams test 100% of a control population instead of a sample
problem: Procedures such as vendor bank-detail changes and deposit reconciliations are tested on a sample, manual review misses digits, and tying hundreds of documents takes hours.
approach: Armanino's risk-advisory team used DataSnipper tools on live client engagements to extract account numbers and terms and match them to documents.
A manager said the team tested 100% of vendor bank and payment-detail changes, versus a 1-of-25 sample (vendor-published).
A manager estimated about 25-plus hours saved on one deposit reconciliation (vendor-published estimate).
The auditor reviews each suggested match and keeps sign-off.

title: Year-round control testing replaces a single point-in-time SOX test cycle
problem: Testing bundled into one point in time finds issues late, and fixes are rushed near year end.
approach: Klaviyo's VP of Internal Audit says agent-run tests let the team test all year, catching issues earlier (vendor-published, no metric).
KPMG argues continuous testing needs continuous evidence collection, which may give a faster return than automating tests.
Control owners work exceptions; auditors review exceptions and the reliability of the monitoring.

title: Continuous first-line controls monitoring with human-approved auto-clear rules (partly an idea)
problem: Periodic, sample-based testing leaves blind spots that surface at year end, and detective controls find issues after the fact.
approach: Grant Thornton describes AI that monitors more transactions continuously, with alerts and human-approved logic setting when AI may auto-clear an item.
KPMG's 2030 view describes embedded, increasingly self-healing controls; a Havertys audit leader expects controls could one day be tested at each occurrence.
No outcome of continuous monitoring is published.
Humans approve the auto-clear logic; control owners triage exceptions and internal audit tests the monitoring.

title: AI pre-review of workpapers, scope and draft findings before human sign-off
problem: Manager review of workpapers is slow and inconsistent, and scope or draft-finding gaps are often found late, so unsupported findings can reach the client.
approach: FJ Management's head of internal audit says Optro lets the team analyse workpapers and run calibrated reviews with a human in loop.
Baker Tilly uses approved custom GPTs to challenge scope, risk-control mapping and whether a draft finding is supported; no measure is published.
The assigned auditor owns the conclusion, and a human reviewer signs off every workpaper.

title: AI drafts audit observations: finding detail, root cause, impact and recommendation
problem: Writing structured observation language after testing is slow and varies by author.
approach: RSM describes an agent that drafts structured observation language from documented test results.
A Gartner poll finds 60% of audit professionals use generative AI to draft audit issues, ratings or reports (independent).
The auditor validates each draft finding, its rating and its root cause with the auditee before the report is final.

title: Reading vendors' SOC reports and assessing vendor AI risk, with agents announced
problem: Clients obtain AI through vendors, and existing SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports may say little about model behaviour, retraining or prompt controls.
approach: KPMG lists SOC report review as an agent type; Optro announced an agentic third-party risk workflow for onboarding and due diligence.
The advisor reads each vendor's SOC report for AI coverage and maps gaps to contract terms and the client's own testing.
A survey reports 40% of audit functions evaluate vendor AI governance and 50% review SOC reports (vendor-published).
Advisor and client owner sign off the gap mapping.

title: Mid-market firms move internal-audit and certification engagements onto one agentic platform
problem: Risk-advisory engagements run on email and spreadsheets, with requests chased by hand and methodology applied inconsistently.
approach: Aprio standardised SOC, ISO, HITRUST and PCI work on Fieldguide from December 2025, and announced agent co-development on 2026-08-05.
Cherry Bekaert announced on 2026-06-03 it would centralise audit, internal audit and SOC work on the platform; Baker Tilly uses it.
No measured result is published; the firms describe intended benefits (self-reported).
Human oversight is stated at each stage of the engagement.

title: A company moves outsourced SOX testing to agents, starting with IT (Havertys)
problem: Havertys paid outside testers to run IT SOX tests; tester turnover is a risk, and the spend buys testing hours rather than advice.
approach: Havertys is adding Optro Autonomous Testing on its Optro SOX system, starting with IT controls it already outsources.
It plans to move to business-process controls and operational audits once IT controls are tested autonomously.
It will judge success partly by how its controls spend shifts toward advisory work; no result yet (vendor-published).
Managers continue to review and approve the work.

title: AI-native providers sell agent-run SOX and internal-audit testing to enterprise audit teams
problem: Public companies spend heavily on SOX testing and it stays manual; Midship cites roughly $2.3 million a year (an unsourced vendor figure).
approach: Vendors sell agents that follow an audit plan, gather evidence, test controls and produce review-ready workpapers; Petual names Navan as a customer.
Petual reports efficiency gains of 68% to 80% on existing SOX workflows (vendor claim); Andera markets a 70% time saving.
Midship raised a $4.15M seed (2026-01-27) for agents that run SOX testing lifecycles.
Built-in approval workflows keep humans in the loop.

title: SOX and internal-audit teams become controls advisers as automation moves earlier
problem: SOX and internal-audit teams spend most capacity testing controls after the fact, while stakeholders ask for advice before controls fail.
approach: KPMG's SOX leader says auditor reliance is going to go away and the role becomes much more of a controls adviser.
KPMG's path forward: embed controls in first-line workflows, build audit-ready evidence by design, and shift to controls advisory.
A poll finds two-thirds of SOX leaders were asked to add value in operational and technology audits; 13% remain fully SOX-focused (independent).
The controller or process owner owns control design; SOX and internal audit advise and test.

title: AI governance, control design and certification-readiness advisory for clients
problem: Clients deploy AI faster than they document ownership, controls and evidence; a KPMG survey finds fewer than half of organisations are fully assurance-ready.
approach: Firms sell design of AI governance, using COSO's February 2026 roadmap: inventory each AI use, assess risk, map controls and set metrics.
Grant Thornton LLP launched an assurance practice on 2026-09-23 with provisional accreditation for AIUC-1 certification of agentic AI controls.
On 2026-10-19 the AICPA and the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company announced a joint SOC 2 plus AIUC-1 offering.
A partner reviews the risk assessment before release; the client control owner confirms each control is operated.
who: COSO, Grant Thornton, RSM, AICPA, KPMG survey

title: AI inventory, shadow-AI discovery and review of user-built automations for a client
problem: Teams cannot govern AI they have not listed, and shadow AI starts outside formal oversight; a LexisNexis report says 54% of consultants use AI tools without approval.
approach: The advisor scans for unsanctioned use, then builds an inventory classifying each use by capability type, with an owner and criticality.
Optro announced intake that pre-populates AI system records; its shadow-AI discovery feature is previewing ahead of 2027 availability.
A governance committee classifies and approves each discovered use; user-built agents pass a review gate before touching production data.

title: Internal-audit review of a client's AI governance (Grant Thornton, global bank)
problem: Traditional AI governance assumes risk is handled before deployment, but agents decide at run time; internal audit needs a repeatable way to test it.
approach: Grant Thornton helped a global bank's auditors build a repeatable, NIST-aligned approach to evaluating AI; the client completed its first lifecycle audit.
Grant Thornton reports seven governance domains under audit and 100+ production use cases validated (self-reported).
AI is the subject of the audit, not the auditor; the internal-audit lead approves scope and finding ratings.
who: Grant Thornton, a global bank, the IIA

title: SOX teams scope and evaluate the AI embedded in clients' business controls
problem: Business teams put AI inside revenue, procure-to-pay and close workflows, and SOX teams have no agreed way to scope or test those controls.
approach: SOX teams ask about AI use in walkthroughs, send control owners quarterly questionnaires and write baseline human-in-the-loop requirements, starting from COSO's guidance.
An informal webinar poll implies 95% of SOX programs lack a defined framework for AI in controls (independent).
Control owners document human-in-the-loop procedures; the SOX team confirms evidence expectations with the external auditor.

title: Idea: written controls before a client's finance agents go live
problem: Idea, not a deployment: close and reconciliation agents are reaching production while finance teams document controls slower than they deploy.
approach: A practitioner proposes a signed memo before an agent touches a production close: inventory, replayable evidence, sign-off gates, assurance mapping, exit threshold.
A validation period is built into the rollout; vendor match-rate and time-saving figures are treated as marketing until reproduced.
The controller signs the memo; a named human owns each agent's output.

title: Idea: AI-enabled fraud readiness and fraud-risk program design for clients
problem: Idea, not a deployment: internal-audit leaders see AI-enabled fraud, such as deepfakes and fabricated documents, as a growing risk, and few feel prepared.
approach: Practitioners discuss advisers helping clients assess exposure to AI-enabled fraud, build skills, update fraud risk assessments and design controls.
Reference points include DOJ's September 2024 compliance guidance on AI risk and FinCEN's November 2024 deepfake alert.
Fraud-risk conclusions remain with management and audit leadership.

title: Idea: certify AI testing tools before use with a parallel run
problem: Idea, not a deployment: no public parallel-run, override or error-rate result exists for AI in internal audit or SOX testing.
approach: Run the tool in shadow mode on completed engagements, compare its results with the team's conclusions, then ramp gradually.
The UK FRC describes testing default and edge cases, recertifying after material changes, and running alternative procedures in parallel.
A named reviewer compares tool output with prior conclusions before any live cutover.
